tutor_context: Key facts: Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Order criteria in SA are that the person has or appears to have a mental illness, the illness requires immediate treatment, there is a risk to the person's or others' health or safety, and no less restrictive means are reasonably available. The order is made on the prescribed form, lasts up to 7 days, requires the patient to be given a copy and a statement of rights, notification to the Chief Psychiatrist, and examination by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner within 24 hours (video assessment is permitted). Misconceptions: that voluntary patients can never be stopped from leaving; that IM sedation is a substitute for lawful detention; that police are the first call for an inpatient. Out of scope: Level 2 and 3 orders and community treatment orders.
plan: Tests prioritisation overnight when a voluntary inpatient becomes psychotic and unsafe: safety first with least restrictive means, then urgent escalation about an inpatient treatment order. Distractors: let her leave, sedate to prevent leaving, call police. Supported by the SA Chief Psychiatrist guideline on Level 1 orders and the Mental Health Act 2009.

stem: You are the intern at a regional hospital with a small medical ward, no intensive care, on-site CT during business hours only, and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air. A 55-year-old man was brought in by police at 14:00 after his wife found him in the shed with a rope. The general practitioner on duty assessed him, found severe depression with a fixed plan to end his life, and made a Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Order under the Mental Health Act 2009 at 15:00 before leaving for the day. He is now settled on the medical ward with one-to-one nursing, has been given a copy of the order and the statement of rights, and the Chief Psychiatrist notification has been sent. At 22:00 the nurse asks you which of the outstanding tasks must be done tonight. The on-call doctor is available by phone, and the Rural and Remote Mental Health Service psychiatrist can assess by video.
lead_in: Which task is most time-critical for you to arrange tonight?

options.text: Examination by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner by video before 15:00 tomorrow to confirm or revoke the order
A full admission clerking with bloods, ECG and chest X-ray before the morning ward round
Booking a non-urgent ambulance for transfer to an Adelaide mental health unit tomorrow afternoon
Writing to his general practitioner to arrange follow-up after discharge

explanations.A: Correct. Under the SA Mental Health Act 2009 a Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Order made by a medical practitioner who is not a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner must be followed by examination of the patient by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner within 24 hours, who confirms or revokes it. In a regional hospital this is arranged through the Rural and Remote Mental Health Service, usually by video, and the Act expressly allows audiovisual examination. Missing the deadline leaves the detention without a lawful basis, so the referral must be made tonight.
explanations.B: A medical clerking is good practice and should happen, but it has no statutory deadline and he is physically well with one-to-one nursing; it can be completed in the morning.
explanations.C: Transfer to an approved treatment centre depends on bed availability and the psychiatrist's decision; booking it is not time-critical tonight and does not replace the statutory examination.
explanations.D: Discharge planning is important but is days away and has no bearing on the lawfulness of his current detention.

learning_point: A Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Order made by a non-psychiatrist must be followed by examination by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner within 24 hours; in regional South Australia this is arranged urgently through the rural mental health service, usually by video.
setting_note: In Adelaide the examination is done in person by the on-site psychiatry team; in a regional hospital the junior doctor must actively arrange the video assessment with the Rural and Remote Mental Health Service and should confirm the time of the order so the 24-hour window is not missed.
presentation: involuntary treatment under the Mental Health Act

generation.uncertainty_note: The 24-hour examination requirement for Level 1 orders made by non-psychiatrists is as understood from the Mental Health Act 2009 (SA) as amended; reviewers should confirm against the current Chief Psychiatrist guideline.

references.title: SA Health, Office of the Chief Psychiatrist: Mental Health Act 2009 - Level 1 Inpatient Treatment Orders guideline
references.locator: Examination within 24 hours by a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner; use of audiovisual conferencing

references.title: Mental Health Act 2009 (SA)
references.locator: Part 5 Division 2: Level 1 inpatient treatment orders - examination and confirmation

tutor_context: Key facts: a Level 1 order lasts up to 7 days; the patient must receive a copy and a statement of rights; the Chief Psychiatrist must be notified; if the order was made by someone other than a psychiatrist or authorised medical practitioner, examination within 24 hours by one of those is required and the order can be confirmed or revoked; examination by audiovisual link is permitted. Patients should be transferred to an approved treatment centre as soon as practicable. Misconceptions: that medical clerking is the overnight priority; that the order stands for 7 days without review. Out of scope: Level 2 orders and SACAT review.
plan: Tests a PGY1 at difficulty 4 on which statutory step is time-critical after a GP makes a Level 1 order in a regional hospital: the 24-hour examination, arranged by video. Distractors are reasonable tasks without a deadline (clerking, transfer booking, GP letter). Supported by the Chief Psychiatrist Level 1 ITO guideline and the Mental Health Act 2009 (SA).

stem: You are the intern in the outpatient clinic of a regional hospital with a small medical ward, no intensive care, and retrieval to Adelaide by road or air; the physician is reviewing another patient and the on-call physician is reachable by phone. A 47-year-old woman is referred by her general practitioner with weight loss. She has a long history of anorexia nervosa and has restricted her intake to a few hundred calories a day for the past 3 weeks, losing 8 kg in 2 months. Her weight is 39 kg (body mass index 14.3). She is orthostatic (lying blood pressure 92/58, standing 76/50), heart rate 42, temperature 35.4. Bloods taken this morning show potassium 2.9 mmol/L, phosphate 0.6 mmol/L, magnesium 0.6 mmol/L, sodium 134 mmol/L. She says she feels fine and would prefer to manage at home with the dietitian.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Provide a high-energy meal plan to follow at home and review her in clinic in one week
Prescribe oral potassium and phosphate supplements and review her in 48 hours
Admit her today for monitored refeeding, electrolyte replacement and thiamine, after discussing with the physician
Refer her to the community eating disorder service for outpatient dietitian review

explanations.A: Starting unsupervised full feeding at home in a severely malnourished patient with low phosphate is the classic setting for refeeding syndrome, with risk of arrhythmia, heart failure and death.
explanations.B: Her bradycardia, hypothermia, postural hypotension and electrolyte derangement are markers of medical instability that need inpatient monitoring; oral replacement and review in 2 days is unsafe.
explanations.C: Correct. A body mass index below 15, rapid weight loss, minimal intake for more than a week, bradycardia below 50, hypothermia and low potassium, phosphate and magnesium place her at high risk of refeeding syndrome and of cardiac complications. National and RANZCP guidance is admission for medical stabilisation: cardiac monitoring, correction of electrolytes, thiamine before and during refeeding, cautious nutrition started at a low rate with daily electrolytes. The intern should discuss with the physician today and not let her go home.
explanations.D: Community eating disorder services are essential for ongoing care but cannot provide the monitoring she needs now; outpatient referral is the next step after medical stabilisation.

learning_point: Severe malnutrition with bradycardia, hypothermia, postural hypotension or low potassium, phosphate or magnesium means high refeeding risk and medical instability: admit for monitored refeeding with electrolyte replacement and thiamine.
setting_note: A regional hospital without intensive care can begin stabilisation but should discuss early with the on-call physician and the statewide eating disorder service about transfer to Adelaide for cardiac monitoring if bradycardia or electrolytes worsen; a tertiary hospital would admit directly to a medical ward with telemetry.
presentation: refeeding risk in an eating disorder

references.title: RANZCP Clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of eating disorders (2014)
references.locator: Indications for medical admission and management of refeeding risk

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
references.locator: Eating disorders - medical complications and refeeding syndrome

references.title: National Eating Disorders Collaboration (NEDC): Eating disorders - a professional resource for general practitioners
references.locator: Medical indicators for hospital admission

tutor_context: Key facts: refeeding syndrome is driven by insulin-induced intracellular shifts of phosphate, potassium and magnesium when carbohydrate is reintroduced; high-risk features include BMI under 16, weight loss over 15 percent in 3-6 months, minimal intake for over 10 days, and low baseline electrolytes. Admission indicators also include heart rate under 50 awake, systolic under 90 or postural drop over 20 mmHg, temperature under 35.5, and ECG abnormalities. Give thiamine before feeding, replace electrolytes, start nutrition cautiously with daily bloods for the first week. Misconceptions: that the patient feeling fine is reassuring; that oral supplements suffice; that a low BMI alone defines risk.
plan: Tests the basic decision to admit a medically unstable patient with anorexia nervosa for monitored refeeding, from an outpatient clinic in a regional hospital. Distractors: home meal plan, oral supplements with early review, community referral. Supported by the RANZCP eating disorder guidelines, Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic and the NEDC resource.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital with a registrar on site overnight. A 70-year-old man is brought in by ambulance at 23:30 after his neighbour found him in the bathroom with cuts to his left forearm. The lacerations are superficial and have stopped bleeding under a dressing. He is tearful and says he wanted to die after his wife went into residential care. On further questioning he says that about 90 minutes before cutting himself he swallowed a handful of his wife's amitriptyline tablets, perhaps 20 of 50 mg. He is drowsy but rousable, heart rate 112, blood pressure 108/70, pupils dilated, mucous membranes dry. The nurse has placed him in a cubicle and asks whether you want to suture the arm first or call the mental health team, as both are waiting.
lead_in: What should you do first?

options.text: Suture the forearm lacerations and then take a detailed mental health history
Move him to a monitored bed, obtain a 12-lead ECG and inform the ED registrar of the amitriptyline ingestion now
Refer him to the mental health team for an urgent risk assessment before any medical investigations
Give activated charcoal and wait for the paracetamol level before deciding further

explanations.A: Superficial lacerations with haemostasis are not urgent; spending 30 minutes suturing while a tricyclic overdose evolves could mean missing the window to treat a widening QRS, seizures or arrhythmia.
explanations.B: Correct. A 1 g amitriptyline ingestion is potentially lethal: anticholinergic signs and tachycardia are already present and sodium channel blockade can cause broad-complex arrhythmia, seizures and hypotension within hours. The first priority is a monitored area, 12-lead ECG looking at QRS duration and the terminal R wave in aVR, intravenous access, and immediate escalation to the registrar so that sodium bicarbonate, airway planning and Poisons Information Centre advice can be arranged. The lacerations and psychiatric assessment follow once he is medically safe.
explanations.C: Mental health assessment is essential but cannot be done meaningfully in a drowsy patient and would delay life-saving monitoring; every self-harm presentation needs medical stabilisation before psychiatric review.
explanations.D: Charcoal is reasonable within an hour in an alert patient with a protected airway, but he is drowsy 90 minutes post-ingestion, and waiting on a paracetamol level is not the time-critical issue; the ECG and monitoring are.

learning_point: In any self-harm presentation, medical risk comes first: a tricyclic antidepressant overdose needs immediate cardiac monitoring, a 12-lead ECG and escalation before wound care or psychiatric assessment.
setting_note: In a regional hospital the same priorities apply with the Poisons Information Centre on 13 11 26 and early retrieval discussion, because tricyclic toxicity can require intubation and intensive care that the hospital cannot provide.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology and Toxinology
references.locator: Tricyclic antidepressant poisoning - risk assessment, ECG monitoring and sodium bicarbonate

references.title: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm (2016)
references.locator: Medical assessment and stabilisation before psychosocial assessment

tutor_context: Key facts: tricyclic ingestion over 10 mg/kg is potentially life-threatening; warning ECG features are QRS over 100 ms (seizure risk) and over 160 ms (arrhythmia risk), and an R wave over 3 mm in aVR; treatment is sodium bicarbonate 1-2 mmol/kg for QRS widening or hypotension, benzodiazepines for seizures, early intubation and hyperventilation if severe. Always ask about co-ingestants and take a paracetamol level, but do not let it dictate the sequence. Misconceptions: wounds first because they are visible; psychiatry first because of the stated intent; assuming an elderly man's overdose is minor. Out of scope: detailed ventilation strategy.
plan: Tests prioritisation in a self-harm presentation where a hidden tricyclic overdose outranks the visible wounds and the psychiatric referral. Metro ED with a registrar on site, so escalation is in person. Distractors: suture first, mental health first, charcoal and wait. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Toxicology and the RANZCP self-harm guideline.

stem: You are the intern in the emergency department of a metropolitan general hospital on a busy night with a registrar on site. A 69-year-old man presents at 23:00 asking for something to help him sleep. His wife died 4 months ago and he lives alone; his daughter is interstate. He has been drinking a bottle of wine most nights, has lost 6 kg, and says he has not slept properly in weeks. When you ask directly, he says he often thinks he would be better off dead and has thought about taking his late wife's leftover morphine tablets, which are still in the house; he has not set a date and says he came in instead because he was frightened by the thought. He has no prior psychiatric history. The registrar, who is managing a resuscitation, suggests over the phone that you give him some temazepam and ask his GP to follow up.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Prescribe a small supply of temazepam and arrange general practitioner review within 48 hours as suggested
Ask him to agree to a no-harm contract and discharge him with the crisis line number
Phone his daughter to arrange for the morphine to be removed from the house and then discharge him
Tell the registrar you assess him as high risk and arrange an urgent mental health assessment before any discharge

explanations.A: A hypnotic would add a means of overdose and does not address the risk. The registrar's suggestion was made without the information you now have; an intern must escalate the new finding rather than follow the original plan.
explanations.B: No-harm contracts have no evidence of reducing suicide and can give false reassurance; discharging a high-risk patient with a phone number alone is unsafe.
explanations.C: Restricting access to means is a valuable part of a safety plan, but it is not sufficient on its own for a man with active suicidal thoughts, a potential method, recent bereavement, alcohol use and social isolation.
explanations.D: Correct. Older men, recently bereaved, living alone, drinking heavily, with weight loss, insomnia and suicidal thoughts that include an identified method, are at high risk of suicide. The right step is graded assertiveness: tell the registrar clearly what you have found and that you believe he needs an urgent mental health assessment in the department tonight, and ensure he is kept safe in the department until that assessment is done. Means restriction and family involvement form part of the subsequent safety plan.

learning_point: Suicidal thoughts with an identified method in an older bereaved man who drinks and lives alone indicate high risk; escalate assertively to the senior doctor and arrange urgent mental health assessment before any discharge.
setting_note: In a regional hospital without an on-site mental health team the same assessment is arranged through the state mental health triage line and the on-call doctor, with the patient kept safe in the department or admitted overnight rather than sent home.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
references.locator: Suicide and deliberate self-harm - risk assessment and immediate management

references.title: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm (2016)
references.locator: Assessment of suicide risk and decisions about discharge

references.title: AMC National Framework for Prevocational Medical Training: Outcome statements
references.locator: 1.1 graded assertiveness and escalation; 2.4 working within limits of expertise

tutor_context: Key facts: older men have the highest suicide rate in Australia; bereavement, living alone, alcohol use, insomnia, weight loss and access to means are risk factors; coming in because he was frightened is a protective sign but does not lower the acute risk. Risk assessment covers ideation, plan, intent, means, previous attempts, protective factors and a mental state examination. Misconceptions: no-harm contracts work; a phone number is a safety plan; a senior's plan made with incomplete information must be followed. Out of scope: antidepressant initiation.
plan: Tests prioritisation and graded assertiveness: the intern uncovers high suicide risk after the registrar has suggested a quick discharge. Metro ED at night. Distractors: follow the hypnotic plan, no-harm contract, means restriction alone. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic, the RANZCP self-harm guideline and the AMC outcome statements.

stem: You are the junior doctor on the medical ward of a rural hospital on the Yorke Peninsula, where a 4-bed emergency department is staffed overnight by one junior doctor with the GP on call. A 36-year-old woman was admitted last night after taking 20 tablets of paracetamol following an argument with her partner; she is receiving acetylcysteine and is medically stable. The mental health triage service will assess her by video this afternoon. The nurse looking after her asks you, while you are reviewing her history together, which part of the history matters most for her future risk of dying by suicide. The history includes a previous overdose 3 years ago requiring admission, full-time work as a teacher, two children aged 8 and 10, and no current alcohol or drug use.
lead_in: Which feature of her history is the strongest predictor of future suicide?

options.text: Her previous suicide attempt
Her age under 40 years
Being female
Her full-time employment

explanations.A: Correct. A previous suicide attempt is consistently the strongest single predictor of future suicide and of repeated self-harm; the year after an attempt carries the highest risk. This history should be prominent in the handover to the mental health team and in discharge planning.
explanations.B: Suicide rates in Australia are highest in middle-aged and older adults, particularly men; age under 40 is not a strong risk marker in itself.
explanations.C: Women attempt self-harm more often, but men die by suicide at about three times the rate; female sex is not a predictor of completed suicide.
explanations.D: Employment and responsibility for children are generally protective factors; unemployment and social isolation increase risk.

learning_point: A previous suicide attempt is the strongest predictor of future suicide; always ask about and document prior attempts and pass them on at handover.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic
references.locator: Suicide and deliberate self-harm - risk factors

references.title: RANZCP Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm (2016)
references.locator: Risk factors for repetition and suicide after self-harm

tutor_context: Key facts: risk factors for suicide include previous attempt, male sex, older age, psychiatric illness (especially depression and substance use), chronic pain or illness, recent loss, social isolation, unemployment, access to lethal means, and family history. Protective factors include dependent children, social connection, employment and help-seeking. Risk stratification tools have poor predictive value; the point of identifying factors is to inform a safety plan and follow-up. Misconceptions: that women are at higher risk of suicide because they self-harm more; that a previous attempt that was 'not serious' can be discounted.
plan: Tests recall of the strongest predictor of future suicide, with a stable inpatient after paracetamol overdose in a rural Yorke Peninsula ward. Distractors are demographic features juniors confuse with risk (young age, female sex) and a protective factor (employment). Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Psychotropic and the RANZCP self-harm guideline.

stem: You are the PGY2 on a term in a general practice linked to a 30-bed regional hospital in South Australia's Mid North, 2 hours by road from Adelaide, with specialist advice by phone. A 22-year-old woman presents with 2 days of light vaginal spotting and intermittent mild left-sided lower abdominal pain. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks ago and a home pregnancy test was positive a week ago. She has had no previous pregnancies, no history of pelvic infection and does not use an intrauterine device. Heart rate 78, blood pressure 118/74, abdomen soft with mild left iliac fossa tenderness and no peritonism. Serum beta-hCG this morning is 1,800 IU/L. A transvaginal ultrasound at the hospital today shows an empty uterus with an endometrial thickness of 12 mm, no adnexal mass, and a trace of free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. The supervising GP asks for your interpretation before you discuss her with the obstetric registrar in Adelaide.
lead_in: What is the most appropriate interpretation of these findings?

options.text: A complete miscarriage, since the uterus is empty and bleeding is light, requiring no further follow-up
A normal early intrauterine pregnancy that is simply too early to see, requiring routine antenatal booking
A pregnancy of unknown location in which ectopic pregnancy has not been excluded
A confirmed ectopic pregnancy requiring immediate transfer to Adelaide for laparoscopy

explanations.A: Complete miscarriage cannot be diagnosed from an empty uterus unless an intrauterine pregnancy was previously confirmed; an empty uterus with a positive hCG may be an ectopic pregnancy.
explanations.B: At an hCG of 1,800 IU/L an intrauterine pregnancy is often, though not always, visible on transvaginal scan; with unilateral pain and free fluid it is unsafe to assume a normal pregnancy and book routine care.
explanations.C: Correct. A positive pregnancy test with no intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy seen on transvaginal ultrasound is a pregnancy of unknown location. With an hCG near the discriminatory zone, unilateral pain and free fluid, ectopic pregnancy must be actively excluded: she is haemodynamically stable, so the plan is a repeat hCG in 48 hours with repeat ultrasound, discussion with the obstetric service, and explicit safety-netting to present immediately with worsening pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizziness or heavy bleeding, bearing in mind the 2-hour distance to definitive surgery.
explanations.D: Ectopic pregnancy has not been confirmed: there is no adnexal mass and she is stable. Immediate transfer for surgery is not justified on these findings, although the threshold for transfer is lower given the distance.

learning_point: A positive hCG with no pregnancy seen on transvaginal ultrasound is a pregnancy of unknown location; ectopic pregnancy must be excluded with serial hCG, repeat ultrasound and clear safety-netting, especially when the patient lives far from surgical care.
setting_note: In a regional practice 2 hours from Adelaide the follow-up plan must be explicit: a named person to review the 48-hour hCG, early discussion with the obstetric registrar, a low threshold for transfer, and advice that any deterioration means calling an ambulance rather than driving; in a metropolitan setting the early pregnancy assessment service would manage the same plan in person.

references.title: Queensland Clinical Guidelines: Early pregnancy loss (Maternity and Neonatal Clinical Guideline)
references.locator: Pregnancy of unknown location - assessment and follow-up

references.title: RANZCOG: Ectopic pregnancy - clinical guidance and statements
references.locator: Diagnosis of ectopic pregnancy and pregnancy of unknown location

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
references.locator: Bleeding in early pregnancy

tutor_context: Key facts: the discriminatory zone for transvaginal ultrasound is commonly quoted as hCG 1,500-2,000 IU/L but is not absolute; in a viable intrauterine pregnancy hCG typically rises by at least 50-60 percent over 48 hours, a plateau or slow rise suggests ectopic, and a fall suggests miscarriage or resolving pregnancy of unknown location. Free fluid raises concern. Anti-D is needed for Rh-negative women with bleeding. Misconceptions: empty uterus equals miscarriage; hCG below the discriminatory zone excludes ectopic; a stable patient does not need safety-netting. Out of scope: methotrexate criteria.
plan: Tests interpretation of a pregnancy of unknown location with features suggestive but not diagnostic of ectopic pregnancy, in a regional general practice where distance makes the follow-up plan critical. Distractors: complete miscarriage, too early to see, confirmed ectopic needing immediate surgery. Supported by the Queensland early pregnancy loss guideline, RANZCOG guidance and Therapeutic Guidelines.

stem: You are the PGY2 in the emergency department of a tertiary hospital in Adelaide. A 31-year-old woman presents at 10:00 on a Sunday asking for emergency contraception after a condom broke during intercourse at about 02:00 on Thursday, around 80 hours ago. She weighs 86 kg (body mass index 31). She is not on any regular contraception, has regular cycles with her last period 12 days ago, takes no other medications, is not breastfeeding and has no history of liver disease or venous thromboembolism. She does not want an intrauterine device. The nearest open pharmacy is some distance away and she asks you to prescribe whatever is most likely to work. You have access to the hospital pharmacy stock.
lead_in: Which emergency contraceptive is most appropriate?

options.text: Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally as a single dose
Ulipristal acetate 30 mg orally as a single dose
Levonorgestrel 1.5 mg orally, repeated after 12 hours
Combined ethinylestradiol and levonorgestrel tablets, two now and two in 12 hours

explanations.A: Levonorgestrel is licensed up to 72 hours and its efficacy falls with time and with higher body weight; at 80 hours in a woman weighing over 70 kg it is clearly inferior to ulipristal.
explanations.B: Correct. Ulipristal acetate 30 mg is effective up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse and is more effective than levonorgestrel at every time point, particularly between 72 and 120 hours and probably in women with higher body weight. Since she declines a copper intrauterine device, which is the most effective option, ulipristal is the best oral choice. She should be advised that it may delay ovulation and her period, that any hormonal contraception started afterwards should be delayed by 5 days, to use condoms meanwhile, and to do a pregnancy test if her period is more than 7 days late.
explanations.C: Doubling the levonorgestrel dose (3 mg) is a strategy some guidelines suggest for women over 70 kg or body mass index over 26 when ulipristal is unavailable, but it is still not recommended beyond 72 hours and ulipristal is available here.
explanations.D: The Yuzpe regimen is less effective than either levonorgestrel or ulipristal and causes more nausea; it has no place when dedicated products are available.

learning_point: Ulipristal acetate 30 mg is the most effective oral emergency contraceptive, works up to 120 hours after unprotected intercourse, and is preferred over levonorgestrel after 72 hours or in women of higher body weight; a copper intrauterine device remains the most effective option overall.
setting_note: Ulipristal and levonorgestrel are both available from community pharmacies in Australia without prescription, and SHINE SA and regional pharmacies can provide them; a regional hospital may not stock ulipristal, in which case double-dose levonorgestrel within 72 hours or referral for a copper intrauterine device are the alternatives.

generation.uncertainty_note: Evidence on body weight and ulipristal efficacy is less certain than for levonorgestrel; Australian guidance still favours ulipristal at 72-120 hours regardless of weight.

references.title: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health
references.locator: Emergency contraception - choice of method and timing

references.title: Australian Medicines Handbook
references.locator: Ulipristal - emergency contraception; Levonorgestrel - emergency contraception

references.title: Family Planning Alliance Australia / SHINE SA: Emergency contraception clinical guidance
references.locator: Ulipristal versus levonorgestrel and body weight considerations

tutor_context: Key facts: copper IUD is the most effective emergency contraception (failure under 0.1 percent) and can be inserted up to 5 days after intercourse or ovulation; ulipristal 30 mg works to 120 hours; levonorgestrel 1.5 mg to 72 hours (some use to 96 hours with reduced efficacy), with a doubled dose considered for weight over 70 kg or BMI over 26. Ulipristal is reduced in efficacy by progestogens taken in the following 5 days, and breastfeeding should be paused for a week. Neither oral method is abortifacient. Misconceptions: that 72 hours is the limit for all oral methods; that the Yuzpe regimen is still standard; that emergency contraception is contraindicated in obesity. Both oral agents are pharmacist-only medicines in Australia.
plan: Tests recall at difficulty 4 of the preferred oral emergency contraceptive beyond 72 hours in a woman of higher body weight who declines an IUD. Metro ED with pharmacy stock available. Distractors: standard levonorgestrel, doubled levonorgestrel, Yuzpe regimen. Supported by Therapeutic Guidelines Sexual and Reproductive Health, the AMH and family planning guidance.
